title: Fifteen remote M5.5+ events occupied 13 grid cells in six days after the 11 April 2012 earthquake in a ComCat snapshot
abstract: We tested the spatial spread of remote earthquakes after the 11 April 2012 Indian Ocean M8.6 earthquake. A fixed ComCat snapshot has 15 preferred-magnitude M5.5+ events more than 1,500 km away in the next six days. They occupy 13 five-degree cells. An exact circular-year time-origin test keeps the 2012 event times and places fixed. The upper-tail fractions are 1.09% for event count and 0.87% for occupied cells. The event count is 2.19 times the same-year null mean. Grid, distance and depth checks retain high six-day counts, but a three-day check is less unusual. The result shows a coarse spatial anomaly under this reference. It does not prove remote triggering. Prior selection of the earthquake and window, mixed preferred magnitudes, one revised catalog, grid effects and the uniform annual origin assumption limit inference. Code, source hashes, all aggregate results, exact null distributions, an independent numerical audit and a figure are included. External event records remain outside the package.

display.caption: Exact circular-year reference distributions for six-day event and occupied-cell counts. Red lines show the observed counts after the 11 April 2012 earthquake. Tail fractions are conditional and retrospective.

citations.reason: Published event, remote-distance floor and six-day window define this retrospective spatial count check.
Systematic remote-triggering study gives prior context; our catalog, null and endpoint differ.
Published pair-cancellation warning informs statistic choice. The same shared source snapshot is used; this is not independent data confirmation.
